L458: ###### Theorem 3.13.
L459: 
L460: With the same assumptions as in cite55†3.11 . There is an isomorphism of linear categories $\Bbbk[\mathcal{C}(S)]^{\op}\simeq\mathcal{L}(\Bbbk S)$.
L461: ###### Proof.
L462: Define a functor of $\Bbbk$-linear categories $\mathcal{F}:\Bbbk[\mathcal{C}(S)]\to\mathcal{L}(\Bbbk S)$ in the following way. On objects, $\mathcal{F}(e)=\Bbbk\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}(e)$ and $\mathcal{F}(C(\alpha))=r_{\alpha}$ defines $\mathcal{F}$ on the bases of the hom-sets. The argument in cite53†3.9 shows that $\mathcal{F}$ is a contravariant functor of $\Bbbk$-linear categories. It is clearly a bijection on objects and cite56†3.12 shows that $\mathcal{F}$ is an isomorphism of hom-sets. ∎
L463: cite57†3.13 shows that up to taking the opposite category, $\Bbbk[\mathcal{C}(S)]$ is isomorphic to a Peirce decomposition of $\Bbbk S$. The key fact is in the proof of cite56†3.12 . If the generalized right ample identity holds, all homomorphisms between the projective modules $\Bbbk\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}(e)$ and $\Bbbk\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}(f)$ are linear combinations of functions of the form $r_{\alpha}$ and only for elements $\alpha\in S$ which satisfy $\alpha^{+}=e$ and $\alpha^{\ast}=f$.
L464: Therefore $\mathcal{L}(\Bbbk S)$ is (the opposite of) the linearization of $\mathcal{C}(S)$ itself. In fact, we can think of the associated category $\mathcal{C}(S)$ as being a “discrete” Peirce decomposition of the semigroup $S$ itself.
L465: ## 4 Examples
L466: A good way to show that the generalized right ample condition is a natural property is to give some natural examples of semigroups which satisfy it. If the set of idempotents $E$ is a subband of $S$, it is shown in [cite23†28 ] that the generalized right ample identity reduces to the well-studied “standard” right ample identity. So we are interested in examples where $E$ is not a subband of $S$.
L467: One important example - the Catalan monoid - was already given in [cite23†28 ] (and will be recalled in the sequel as well).
L468: In this section we give two additional examples of such semigroups.
L469: ### 4.1 Linear operators on a Hilbert space ^{1}^{1} 1 This example is part of the ArXiv version of [cite23†28 ] but was omitted from the final paper due to referee’s request.

L497: ###### Remark 4.2.
L498: The reader might be disappointed by an example where $\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}_{E}=\Lc$ and $\widetilde{\mathcal{R}}_{E}=\Rc$ because in this case the congruence and the generalized ample conditions reduce to known facts on Green’s relations (and this is also the situation in the next example in this section). L500: ### 4.2 Order-preserving functions with a fixed point
L501: 
L502: Let $\T_{n}$ be the monoid of all functions $f:[n]\to[n]$ (where $[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}$). A function is called order-preserving if $i_{1}\leq i_{2}$ implies $f(i_{1})\leq f(i_{2})$. Denote by $\Op_{n}$ the monoid of all order-preserving functions $f:[n]\to[n]$. We denote by $\OF_{n}$ the monoid of all order-preserving functions $f:[n]\to[n]$ with the fixed point $f(n)=n$.
L503: ###### Example 4.3.

L510: 2&3&3\end{array}\right)$$  |

L514: 3&3&3\end{array}\right)$$  |
L515: Clearly, $\OF_{n}$ is a submonoid of $\Op_{n}$. Note the analogy with the definition of the monoid $\PT_{n}$ of all partial functions on an $n$-element set. The monoid $\PT_{n}$ can be identified with the submonoid of $\T_{n+1}$ which consists of all functions $f:[n+1]\to[n+1]$ such that $f(n+1)=n+1$.
L516: To the author’s knowledge, the monoid $\OF_{n}$ has not been studied before. In this section we will discuss some properties of this monoid with emphasis on its structure as a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup.

Since $f$ is order-preserving, the kernel classes of $f$ are intervals - if $i_{1}\leq i_{2}\leq i_{3}$ and $(i_{1},i_{3})\in\ker(f)$ then $(i_{1},i_{2})\in\ker f$ also.

L534: Another observation will be useful. A function $f:[n]\to[n]$ is called order-increasing if $i\leq f(i)$ for every $i\in[n]$. In particular, if $f$ is order-increasing then $f(n)=n$. Let $\C_{n}$ be the submonoid of $\OF_{n}$ which consists of all order-preserving and order-increasing functions $f:[n]\to[n]$. This monoid is called the Catalan monoid because the size of $\C_{n}$ is the $n$-th Catalan number [cite64†8 , Theorem 14.2.8].
L535: It is well-known that $\C_{n}$ is a $\Jc$-trivial monoid [cite34†31 , Proposition 17.17]. Given $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{l}\}$ and $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{l}\}$ we say that $X\leq Y$ if $x_{i}\leq y_{i}$ for $1\leq i\leq l$. L539: #### Idempotents
L540: 
L541: Let $X=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{l}\}$ and $Y=\{y_{1},\ldots,y_{l}\}$ be two subsets of $[n-1]$. L628: ###### Lemma 4.8.

L630: For every field $\Bbbk$ the algebra $\Bbbk\OF_{n}$ is semisimple.
L631: ###### Proof.

L633: It is well-known that the algebra $\Bbbk\mathcal{G}$ of a finite groupoid $\mathcal{G}$ is semisimple if and only if the order of every endomorphism group is invertible in $\Bbbk$ ([cite34†31 , Theorem 8.15]). L634: We remark that not many examples are known for non-inverse semigroups with a semisimple algebra. Another notable example is the semigroup of matrices over a finite field of appropriate characteristic (see [cite34†31 , Section 5.6]).
L635: #### The monoid of order-preserving partial permutations
L636: Recall that the symmetric inverse monoid $\IS_{n}$ is the monoid of all partial permutations on the set $[n]$. Our next observation is related to the submonoid $\IO_{n}$ of all order-preserving partial permutations (also denoted sometimes $\POI_{n}$- see [cite69†4 , cite70†5 , cite71†7 ]). In other words, $\IO_{n}$ consists of all partial permutations $\theta:[n]\to[n]$ such that $\theta(i)<\theta(j)$ if $i,j$ are in the domain of $\theta$ and $i<j$.
L637: It is clear that every $\theta\in\IO_{n}$ is completely determined by its domain and image. In the other direction, given $X,Y\subseteq[n]$ such that $|X|=|Y|$ there exists a unique $\theta_{X,Y}\in\IO_{n}$ whose domain is $X$ and image is $Y$. Therefore, elements of $\IO_{n}$ can also be indexed by pairs of sets $X,Y\subseteq[n]$ such that $|X|=|Y|$.
L638: It is well-known that $\IO_{n}$ is an inverse semigroup so in particular, it is a reduced $E$-Fountain semigroup for $E=E(\IO_{n})$ which satisfies the congruence condition. Moreover, its idempotents commute and it satisfies the left and right ample conditions. Consider the associated category $\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})$ (which is in fact an inductive groupoid - see [cite72†17 , Chapter 4]). It is easy to deduce that the categories $\mathcal{C}(\IO_{n})$ and $\mathcal{C}(\OF_{n+1})$ are isomorphic.
